modules.title: Name the whole
modules.skill: Read a fraction as EQUAL parts of a named whole; the denominator counts the equal parts.

items.title: A ribbon in equal parts
items.story: A ribbon is cut into 8 equal parts. 3 of the parts are red. What fraction is red?

steps.prompt: What is the WHOLE here (what equals 1)?

choices.feedback: Yes — the whole is the complete thing, all 8 equal parts together.
That is only the part we keep, not the whole. The whole is everything.

choices.text: The number 3, because it is said first
choices.feedback: A count of parts is not the whole; the whole is the full shape.

steps.hint: The whole is the full thing before we cut it.

steps.prompt: What number goes on the BOTTOM (the denominator)?

choices.feedback: Right — the whole is in 8 equal parts, so the denominator is 8.
That is the numerator, not the denominator. Bottom = total equal parts.
That counts the leftover parts, not the total parts the whole was cut into.

steps.hint: The denominator counts the EQUAL parts the whole is cut into.

steps.prompt: What number goes on TOP (the numerator)?

choices.feedback: Yes — 3 parts are red, so the top number is 3.
All parts together make the whole (that would be 8/8=1).
Those are the parts that are NOT red. We want the red ones.

steps.hint: The numerator is how many equal parts match the question.

solution.text: The whole is the complete a ribbon, cut into 8 equal parts.

items.explain: Why must the parts be EQUAL before the bottom number counts them?

modules.rule: A fraction a/b means: cut the whole into b EQUAL parts, then take a of them.
modules.transfer: You will reuse 'name the whole' in every later module — percentages too.

modules.title: Part and its complement
modules.skill: From a figure, read shaded vs unshaded; a part and its complement add to the whole.

items.title: Reading the unshaded part
items.story: A rectangle is divided into 8 equal parts; 5 parts are shaded. Write the UNSHADED portion as a fraction.

steps.prompt: How many parts make the WHOLE figure?

choices.feedback: Yes — all 8 equal parts together make the whole, so the denominator is 8.
That counts only the shaded parts, not the whole figure.
That counts only the unshaded parts, not the whole figure.

steps.hint: Count every equal part, shaded and unshaded together.

steps.prompt: How many parts are UNSHADED?

choices.feedback: Right — 3 parts are unshaded.
Careful — those are the shaded parts. The question asks for the unshaded ones.
All parts together are the whole, not just the part asked for.

steps.hint: Match the parts to what the question asks — shaded OR unshaded.

steps.prompt: Which fraction answers the question?

choices.feedback: Yes — 3 out of 8 equal parts is 3/8 = 3/8.
That is the shaded share — the complement, not what was asked.
The bottom must be the total parts; this flips top and bottom.

steps.hint: Put the matching count on top and the total on the bottom.

items.explain: Why do a part and its complement always add up to exactly 1?

modules.title: Equivalent fractions
modules.skill: Make equal fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator AND denominator by the same number.

items.title: Build to twelfths
items.story: Write a fraction equal to 3/4 that has 12 on the bottom.

steps.prompt: To turn the bottom 4 into 12, what do you do?

choices.feedback: Yes — 4 x 3 = 12, so the multiplier is 3.
Adding changes the value. Equivalent fractions come from MULTIPLYING.
That would make the bottom 48, far too big. Use the factor 3.

steps.hint: Find the number that 4 is multiplied by to reach 12.

steps.prompt: What must you do to the TOP to keep the fraction equal?

choices.feedback: Right — multiply top and bottom by the same 3; that is multiplying by 3/3 = 1.
Changing only the bottom changes the value — the fraction would no longer be equal.
Mixing 'multiply bottom, add top' breaks the equality. Multiply BOTH.

steps.hint: Whatever you do to the bottom, do the SAME to the top.

steps.prompt: Which fraction is equal to the original?

choices.feedback: Yes — 3 x 3 = 9 and 4 x 3 = 12, giving 9/12.
This came from ADDING 3 to each — 6/7 is not equal to 3/4.
Only the top was multiplied here; the bottom must change too.

steps.hint: Compute 3 x 3 over 4 x 3.

solution.text: Multiply the top by the same 3: 3 x 3 = 9.

items.explain: Why does multiplying top and bottom by the same number not change the value?

steps.prompt: So how many are in the asked part?

This used the share from dividing by the numerator, so it misses the real count.
That is ALL the marbles; only 3/4 of them are asked for.

steps.hint: Multiply one share by 3.

steps.prompt: To find 4/9 of 63, what is ONE share (one 9th)?

choices.feedback: Right — one 9th of 63 is 63 ÷ 9 = 7.
That divided by the NUMERATOR; one share comes from dividing by the denominator.
Finding a share is division into equal parts, not subtraction.

steps.hint: Divide 63 into 9 equal shares.

steps.prompt: How many of those shares do we take?

choices.feedback: Yes — the numerator 4 tells how many 9ths to take.
Taking all 9 shares would give back the whole 63; take just 4.
One share is only 7; the numerator 4 says take 4 of them.

steps.hint: Take the numerator, 4, of the shares.

steps.prompt: So how many are in the asked part?

choices.feedback: Yes — 7 x 4 = 28 plants.
This used the share from dividing by the numerator, so it misses the real count.
That is ALL the plants; only 4/9 of them are asked for.

steps.hint: Multiply one share by 4.

items.check: Asked part 28 + rest 35 = 63 plants in all.
items.explain: Why does 'of' mean multiply, and why divide by the denominator first?

modules.rule: a/b of N = (N ÷ b) x a — share into b, take a shares.
modules.transfer: Fraction-of-a-quantity is exactly how percentages of amounts work.
teach: 'of' means multiply: a/b of N = a/b x N.
Divide N by the denominator to find one share, then take 'numerator' shares.
Dividing by the numerator only (ignoring the denominator) is the trap.
contrast: x by numerator = how many shares

modules.title: Fraction equations and word problems
modules.skill: Solve missing-number fraction equations and word problems by working back from the whole.

items.title: Library, lab, playground
items.story: In a class, 3/7 of the students went to the library and 2/7 went to the science lab. The remaining 14 students went to the playground. How many went to the library?

steps.prompt: What fraction of the class went to the playground?

choices.feedback: Right — 3/7 + 2/7 = 5/7 left, so 2/7 remain for the playground.
5/7 is the part that went to library and lab TOGETHER, not the remainder.
Subtract both known fractions from 7/7: 7/7 - 3/7 - 2/7 = 2/7, not 1/7.

steps.hint: The three groups together make the whole (7/7).

steps.prompt: 14 students are 2/7 of the class. What is the WHOLE class?

choices.feedback: Yes — one 7th is 14 ÷ 2 = 7, so the whole is 7 x 7 = 49.
That doubled the remainder; instead find one 7th first, then scale to 7 sevenths.
14 is TWO sevenths, not one, so multiply one 7th (which is 7) by 7, giving 49.

steps.hint: If 2/7 is 14, one 7th is 14 ÷ 2.

steps.prompt: How many went to the library (3/7 of 49)?

choices.feedback: Yes — 3/7 of 49 is 3 x 7 = 21 students.
14 is the playground group (2/7), not the library group (3/7).
7 is just one 7th; the library share is 3 sevenths, so 3 x 7 = 21.

steps.hint: One 7th is 7; take 3 of them.

solution.text: 2/7 of the class = 14, so one 7th = 7 and the whole = 49.

items.explain: Why does the leftover count tell us the size of the whole class?

items.title: Filling the water tank
items.story: A water tank is 4/7 full. It needs 120 litres more to fill completely. What is the total capacity of the tank?

steps.prompt: What fraction of the tank is still EMPTY?

choices.feedback: Right — 4/7 is full, so 3/7 is still empty.
4/7 is the FILLED part; the empty part is what the 120 litres will fill.

steps.hint: Full is 7/7; subtract the part already filled.

steps.prompt: 120 litres fill the empty 3/7. How big is one 7th?

choices.feedback: Yes — 3 sevenths hold 120 litres, so one 7th is 40 litres.
That multiplied instead of dividing; one of the 3 sevenths is 120 ÷ 3 = 40.
120 litres fill THREE sevenths together, so one 7th is smaller.

steps.prompt: What is the TOTAL capacity (7 sevenths)?

choices.feedback: Yes — 7 x 40 = 280 litres total capacity.
That is only the filled 4/7; the whole tank is all 7 sevenths.
Recount: one 7th is 40, and 7 x 40 = 280, not 240.

steps.hint: Multiply one 7th by 7.

items.explain: Why does the 'litres needed' describe the EMPTY fraction, not the full one?

items.title: Ajay's bank balance
items.story: Ajay withdrew Rs. 2700, which is 3/5 of the money in his account. What is the balance left after the withdrawal?

steps.prompt: Rs. 2700 is 3/5 of the total. What is one 5th?

choices.feedback: Right — 3 fifths are 2700, so one 5th is 2700 ÷ 3 = 900.
That multiplied; one of the 3 fifths is 2700 ÷ 3 = 900.
2700 covers THREE fifths together, so one 5th is smaller.

steps.prompt: What fraction of the money is LEFT after withdrawing 3/5?

choices.feedback: Yes — 5/5 - 3/5 = 2/5 remains in the account.
3/5 is what was taken OUT; the balance is what stays in.
After a withdrawal the whole amount is no longer there; 2/5 remains.

steps.hint: Whole is 5/5; subtract the withdrawn 3/5.

steps.prompt: So what is the balance (2/5 of the total)?

choices.feedback: Yes — 2/5 of the total is 2 x 900 = Rs. 1800.
4500 is the TOTAL before withdrawal, not the balance left.
900 is one fifth; the balance is TWO fifths, so 2 x 900 = 1800.

steps.hint: One 5th is 900; take 2 of them.

items.explain: Why is the balance the COMPLEMENT (2/5), not the withdrawn 3/5?

items.title: The repeated numerator
items.story: The same number fills every box: box/7 + box/7 + box/7 + box/7 = 48/28. What number is the box?

steps.prompt: Simplify the right side, 48/28, to lowest terms.

choices.feedback: Right — the GCD of 48 and 28 is 4, giving 12/7.
That only divided by 2 — keep going: 24/14 = 12/7 in lowest terms.
Both 48 and 28 are even, so it can still be reduced to 12/7.

steps.hint: Divide top and bottom by their GCD.

steps.prompt: Add the four like fractions on the left. What do you get?

choices.feedback: Yes — four copies of box/7 is (4 x box)/7.
Adding like fractions keeps the bottom 7; it does not become 7 x 4 = 28 on top of one box.
All four terms count; together they make (4 x box)/7.

steps.hint: Same bottom 7, so add the tops: box four times.

steps.prompt: Solve (4 x box)/7 = 12/7. What is box?

choices.feedback: Yes — 4 x box = 12, so box = 3.
12 is 4 x box, not box itself; divide by 4 to get 3.
48 was before simplifying; after reducing, 4 x box = 12, so box = 3.

steps.hint: Same bottom, so 4 x box = 12.

items.explain: Why can we compare only the tops once both sides share the denominator 7?

items.title: Numerator tells the denominator
items.story: The numerator of a fraction is 21. The denominator is 16 less than the numerator. Write the fraction as a mixed number.

steps.prompt: What is the denominator?

choices.feedback: Right — 16 less than 21 is 21 - 16 = 5.
16 is the amount you subtract, not the denominator itself.
'16 less than' means subtract 16, not add it.

steps.hint: Denominator = numerator - 16.

steps.prompt: So the fraction is 21/5. Is it proper or improper?

choices.feedback: Yes — the top is larger than the bottom, so 21/5 is improper and makes a mixed number.
Not always; when the top exceeds the bottom the fraction is more than 1.
21 ÷ 5 is 4 with a remainder, so it is 4 and a bit, not exactly 4.

steps.hint: Compare the top with the bottom.

steps.prompt: Convert 21/5 to a mixed number:

choices.feedback: Yes — 5 goes into 21 four times with 1 left over, so 4 1/5.
16 was only the difference; the denominator is 5, so the leftover is over 5.
That is 9/5, far too small; 21/5 is 4 1/5.

steps.hint: 21 ÷ 5 = whole remainder.

items.explain: Why does 'the denominator is 16 less than the numerator' set the bottom, not the leftover?

items.title: Find the missing numerator
items.story: Find the number for the box: 6 + box/8 = 7 3/8.

steps.prompt: Subtract 6 from both sides. What must box/8 equal?

choices.feedback: That dropped the extra whole; 7 3/8 - 6 is 1 3/8, not just 3/8.
7 3/8 - 6 = 1 3/8 exactly; recheck the whole-number part.

steps.hint: 7 3/8 - 6 leaves the fractional part plus one whole.

steps.prompt: Write 1 3/8 as an improper fraction over 8.

choices.feedback: You cannot add the whole straight onto the numerator; 1 = 8/8 first.
That ignored the whole number 1; include 8/8 as well.

steps.hint: 1 whole = 8/8.

steps.prompt: So box/8 = 11/8. What is box?

choices.feedback: Yes — equal bottoms, so box = 11.
8 is the denominator, not the numerator we are solving for.
3 is only the leftover eighths; the whole adds 8 more, giving 11.

steps.hint: Same bottom means the tops match.

items.explain: Why must we turn the whole number into eighths before reading the numerator?

items.title: When will Siddhi finish?
items.story: Siddhi finishes 3/5 of her maths exercise in 24 minutes. She started at 11:00 am. At what time will she finish the whole exercise?

steps.prompt: 3/5 of the work took 24 minutes. How long is one 5th?

choices.feedback: Right — 3 fifths took 24 minutes, so one 5th is 8 minutes.
That multiplied; one of the 3 fifths is 24 ÷ 3 = 8 minutes.
24 minutes covers THREE fifths together, so one fifth is less.

steps.hint: One 5th = 24 ÷ 3.

steps.prompt: How many minutes for the WHOLE exercise (5 fifths)?

choices.feedback: Yes — 5 x 8 = 40 minutes for the full exercise.
24 minutes is only 3/5 of the work, not all of it.
That is only 4 fifths; the whole is 5 fifths, so 8 x 5 = 40.

steps.hint: Multiply one 5th by 5.

steps.prompt: She started at 11:00 am. When does she finish?

choices.feedback: Yes — 11:00 + 40 minutes = 11:40 am.
11:24 is when only 3/5 is done (24 minutes), not the whole exercise.
That added an extra hour; the full task is 40 minutes, not 1 hour 40.

steps.hint: Add 40 minutes to 11:00.

items.check: 24 min done (3/5) + 16 min left (2/5) = 40 min total.
items.explain: Why does finding one 5th first let us scale up to the whole time?

items.title: Counting garden plants
items.story: In a garden, 2/9 of the plants are roses, 1/9 are sunflowers and 4/9 are marigolds. The remaining 30 plants are hibiscus. How many sunflowers and marigolds are there in all?

steps.prompt: What fraction of the plants are hibiscus (the remainder)?

choices.feedback: Right — 2/9 + 1/9 + 4/9 = 7/9, leaving 2/9 for hibiscus.
7/9 is the roses+sunflowers+marigolds together, not the hibiscus remainder.

steps.hint: Subtract the three named fractions from 9/9.

steps.prompt: 30 hibiscus are 2/9 of the garden. How many plants in all?

choices.feedback: Yes — one 9th is 30 ÷ 2 = 15, so the whole is 15 x 9 = 135.
30 is TWO ninths, not one; find one 9th (15) first, then x 9.
That doubled the remainder; the whole is far bigger — 135 plants.

steps.hint: One 9th = 30 ÷ 2, then x 9.

steps.prompt: How many are sunflowers AND marigolds (1/9 + 4/9 of 135)?

choices.feedback: Yes — 5/9 of 135 is 5 x 15 = 75 plants.
30 is the hibiscus group; sunflowers + marigolds are 5 ninths, giving 75.
One 9th is 15; together sunflowers and marigolds are 5 ninths, so 75.

steps.hint: That is 5/9 of 135; one 9th is 15.

solution.text: 2/9 = 30, so one 9th = 15 and the whole = 9 x 15 = 135.

items.explain: Why does the hibiscus remainder unlock the size of the whole garden?

modules.rule: Name the whole, write the fraction relationship, then solve for the unknown.
modules.transfer: This is the reasoning IPM word problems reward most.
teach: In 'remaining = whole - known fractions', the leftover count pins down the whole.
For like-fraction equations, scale the single term up to the target.
For numerator-defined-by-denominator problems, build the numerator from the rule first.
contrast: Find the WHOLE from the leftover
Then take the asked fraction of it
